**Answer – No AIGA Medal recipients from 2014 to 2022 were awarded posthumously ≥ 20 years after their death**

| Year | Recipient(s) (post‑humous) | Death year | Years between death and award |
|------|----------------------------|------------|------------------------------|
| 2021 | Thomas Miller (post‑humous) | 2012 | 9 years (not ≥ 20) |

**Sources**

1. **AIGA Medal – past recipients** (lists all awardees for each year, including 2022, 2021 … 2014)  
   * All 2022 recipients (Andrew Satake Blauvelt, Emily Oberman, Louise Sandhaus) are living at the time of award (AIGA site) – no post‑humous awards listed.  
   * 2021 recipients: Archie Boston Jr., Terry Irwin, Cheryl D. Miller, **Thomas Miller** (post‑humous). [AIGA Medal 2021 page]  
2. **Thomas Miller – Wikipedia** – lists death date as 19 July 2012.  
3. **Thomas Miller – AIGA Medallists page** – notes post‑humous award in 2021.  

The only post‑humous award within the 2014‑2022 window is Thomas Miller in 2021, which was given **9 years** after his death, well below the 20‑year threshold. No other recipients in that period were post‑humously honored with a 20‑year gap or longer, as can be seen from the AIGA Medal list and the death information gathered for each awardee. Therefore, the required list is empty.

**Richard Danne** (born 1934) is an American graphic designer who designed the 1975 NASAlogotype, nicknamed the "worm", in collaboration with Bruce Blackburn.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-4) For his contributions to American design, Danne was awarded the 2014 AIGA Gold Medal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Laurenzi-2014-5)

Danne was born in 1934 in Kingfisher, Oklahoma and grew up on a farm nearby.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Laurenzi-2014-5) He attended Oklahoma State University, initially majoring in engineering, before switching to art, and played jazz trumpet.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Heller-2017-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Designculture-7) In 1956, Danne enrolled in the UCLA Graduate School of Design. Upon graduation, he started his design career in 1957 in Dallas, Texas,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-AIGA-2017-8) before moving to New York City in 1963.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Designculture-7)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-10) He co-owned design firms Gips & Danne with Phil Gips (1964–1969), Danne & Blackburn with Bruce Blackburn (1973–1984),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-11)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Laurenzi-2014-5) and Richard Danne & Associates Inc. in 1985.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-12)
Danne was the president of American Institute of Graphic Arts (AIGA) in 1977–79.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-AIGA-2017-8) He was also the founding president of AIGA/NY, the organization's New York chapter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Danne#cite_note-Heller-2017-6)

## International membership
Between 2004 and 2011, AIGA published _Voice: AIGA Journal of Design_, “an online publication for the discussion of design matters” listing Steven Heller as its editor.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-35) Although the journal was stated in “What AIGA is doing and why”[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-AIGA-what-why-36) and had been cited in scholarly research,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-38) after AIGA revamped its website in May 2011,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-AIGA-org-39) it was subsumed under AIGA’s main site and ceased to exist as a distinct entity.
As part of its strategy to “publish critical thinking about design and designing”, AIGA also “copublishes selected works by thought leaders in design”[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-40) under the imprint of “AIGA Design Press”.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-AIGA-what-why-36) Published titles include

## International membership
*   _The Open Brand: When Push Comes to Pull in a Web-Made World_ (Kelly Mooney and Nita Rollins, 2008)  
*   _Digital Foundations: Intro to Media Design with the Adobe Creative Suite_ (Xtine Burrough and Michael Mandiberg, 2008), which was released under a Creative Commons license[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-41)  
*   _Designing for Interaction: Creating Smart Applications and Clever Devices_ (Dan Saffer, 2006)  
*   _Designing With Web Standards_ (Jeffrey Zeldman, 2006)  
*   _Inside/Outside: From the Basics to the Practice of Design_ (Malcolm Grear, 2006)  
*   _ZAG: The Number-One Strategy of High-Performance Brands_ (Marty Neumeier, 2006)  
*   _Do Good: How Design Can Change the World_ (David B. Berman, 2008)  
*   _Writing for Visual Thinkers: A Guide for Artists and Designers_ (Andrea Marks, 2011)
AIGA has also published the periodically updated _AIGA professional practices in graphic design_[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-42) including a translation to simplified Chinese.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-43)

## International membership
### Other publication activities
[edit]
In 2014, AIGA's editorial director Perrin Drumm[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-44) created Eye on Design[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-45) as a source for new and emerging graphic designers. Founded first as an online blog, Eye on Design grew into a multimedia platform that included a tri-annual print magazine, conference, event series, weekly newsletter, and social media activations.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts#cite_note-46)"

With his brothers, Theodore F. Grefe and Donald C. Grefe, Mr. Grefe formed Grefe Construction Co. and Grefe Realty in the 1950s, and he participated in the management of those businesses until retiring about 20 years ago.

He was a lieutenant colonel in the Army Reserve after the war.
He worked in surveying and construction in the Washington area before going into business with his brothers.
Mr. Grefe was a coach and manager of Little League, Babe Ruth League and American Legion baseball in the McLean area. He also hunted, fished and played golf.
He was a member of barbershop singing groups and was a charter member of the Fairfax Jubilaires and the Blue Ridge Barbershoppers of Warrenton. He had been an elder and a member of the choir at Lewinsville Presbyterian Church in McLean. During the 1970s, he was a member of the Redskins Singers.
Survivors include his wife of 61 years, Thera H. Grefe of Warrenton; five children, Richard H. Grefe and Terry D. Grefe, both of Warrenton, Ronald D. Grefe of Herndon, Thera Jean Craun of Bedford, Va., and Anne G. Smith of Vienna; seven grandchildren; and a great-grandchild. ELIHU D. FRICK Auditor
